title: Labor draws battlelines over purpose of super
full_text:
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has reaffirmed the government’s opposition to policies that would allow Australians to use superannuation for purposes other than retirement, as the debate over linking super and home ownership intensifies.
Delivering a keynote address at a CareSuper and UNSW forum in Sydney, Gallagher said political pressure to broaden access to super remained a threat to the retirement system.
“Obviously, the pushback on super is real, it’s always been a political policy area. It continues to be so… [and] in the Labor government, we will continue to protect and ensure that super isn’t used for other purposes,” Gallagher said.
Her comments followed a renewed push from shadow housing and homelessness minister Andrew Bragg for Australia’s retirement system to prioritise outright home ownership.
Speaking at a media briefing at the Australian Computer Society in Sydney on Tuesday, Bragg argued workers should be able to access their superannuation to buy a first home.
“The IGR says that the housing status is a strong predictor of the success of your retirement, and so none of this will be surprising to you because the economic and psychological benefits of home ownership transcend any other financial interest that you may be able to have,” Bragg said.
“There is nothing wrong with choosing to rent to make that very clear, but we don’t want to make renting in retirement compulsory.”
The Coalition took a policy to the 2022 and 2025 elections that would have allowed Australians to withdraw up to $50,000 from their super to purchase their first home.
Under Bragg’s proposed hierarchy for retirement policy, owning a home outright would take precedence, followed by accumulating income-producing assets capable of supplementing or replacing the Age Pension.
Bragg also questioned the separation of housing and super policy, citing data showing 32 per cent of super lump sums had been used to repay mortgages during the previous year.
The Super Members Council (SMC) opposed using super for housing deposits, warning the policy could increase house prices and rents, reduce retirement savings and raise future reliance on the Age Pension.
Research commissioned by the council in 2025 found allowing first home buyers to withdraw super for a deposit could lift Australian house prices by up to 10.3 per cent.
While Gallagher did not directly touch on Bragg’s housing proposal in her keynote address, she reiterated the government’s broader commitment to ensuring super was preserved for retirement.
However, the minister singled out a separate One Nation proposal to allow workers to redirect 3 per cent of their superannuation contributions into their take-home pay.
“We don’t support the policy from One Nation to divert 3 per cent of the [super] pay packet. [We] agree and accept that it sounds quite popular to many, particularly when pressures are on household budgets,” Gallagher said.
“But we know that whilst you might get $40 a week more on average, it could be $25,000 worse off at retirement, so we’ll continue to push on that.”
Alongside protecting existing contributions, Gallagher identified women’s earnings as a critical driver of retirement outcomes and argued that improving wages would have a long-term effect on super balances.
“If we know that improving wages is the single biggest thing we can do to improve women’s retirement incomes, and so some of the work that we’ve done through the Fair Work Commission with the gender undervaluation case that’s currently working its way through, but also in the pay increases that we’ve done in the aged care and early education and care sector, where significant wage increases in both of those areas will have a profound effect on women’s retirement incomes over time,” she said.
Women’s superannuation gap typically emerges during their 20s and 30s as caring responsibilities prompt some to move from full-time employment into part-time work, Gallagher said.
Changes to the Commonwealth paid parental leave scheme were intended to address one contributor to that gap by ensuring super was paid on the government-funded entitlement.
“Super would be paid in some places on leave without pay as well, but on paid parental leave and on our system that we were the Commonwealth paid parental leave system that we were responsible for, it wasn’t paid on that. So we have addressed that,” she said.
Reforms to the low income super tax offset were also presented as part of the government’s effort to improve women’s retirement outcomes, following advocacy from Women in Super and the SMC.
Gallagher said payday super would further support women by helping ensure their entitlements reached their accounts when due.
“Payday super again, making sure it’s in your own account when it’s meant to be paid will make a big change to women over time, making sure that you know super is paid is also a key thing,” she said.
Broader improvements in women’s workforce participation and earnings were beginning to support financial security, according to Gallagher, who cited Australia’s rise from 43rd to eighth in global gender equality rankings.
“The gender pay gap is at the lowest rate on record. We’ve had the highest participation of women in the labour market [last year]. Women’s average weekly earnings have grown to over $300 per week per week more,” she said.
Despite that progress, Gallagher acknowledged further work was required to address structural inequality and strengthen women’s financial security.
“We’re going to continue to chip away at all of these areas because we believe that when the economy works for women, it works for everybody, and everyone gets the best outcome possible.”
